title: Persona Briefs - Platform Eng vs ML Eng vs Security
path: shared_drives/go-to-market/Persona Briefs - Platform Eng vs ML Eng vs Security.json
content:
Purpose
- Help AEs/SEs quickly choose: (1) which scenario to run first, (2) which proof points to emphasize, (3) when to pivot from Hosted → Dedicated → Private.
- This is intended to be used live (pre-call prep). Keep it simple; don’t try to show everything.

General guidance (applies to all personas)
- Start with ONE “hero” scenario. Use the rest as optional branches.
- Avoid hard numbers unless you’re using the approved ranges from “Benchmark Proof Points - Slides Inputs”. If asked: “We can validate with your prompts + target latency/cost in an eval.”
- For nondeterminism: use the canned prompts + expected outputs; narrate that outputs vary but we focus on reliability, tooling, and serving economics.
- Always have a Plan B: screenshots of Console dashboards + pre-recorded output snippets if live API responses wobble.

Quick picker (2-minute decision)
- Platform/Infra Eng in the room? → Start with Reliability + Routing/Fallback + Dashboards (Console).
- ML Eng / Applied ML lead? → Start with Quality/Structured Output + tool calling OR batch/caching controls (depending on whether they care about correctness vs throughput).
- Security/Compliance lead? → Start with Isolation + Retention + Audit logs + Private/VPC story. Show controls before “cool prompts”.

Call patterns
- 15-min “mini demo” (Hosted API only): streaming chat + quick look at token cost/latency panel.
- 30-min standard: 1 hero scenario + 1 supporting scenario + 2 minutes of deployment modes.
- 45-min enterprise: hero scenario + reliability/fallback + security posture + next steps for eval + success criteria.

========================================
Persona 1: Platform Engineering / Infrastructure ("make it reliable + operable")
========================================
What they’re optimizing for
- Stable production behavior: predictable latency, capacity, error rates.
- Operability: dashboards, tracing hooks, error analysis, rollouts, and blast-radius control.
- Flexibility: “Don’t lock me into one deployment model.”

Primary pain points we should mirror back
- “Our LLM feature is fragile: retries, timeouts, provider outages, region issues.”
- “We can’t explain cost spikes or latency regressions.”
- “We have multiple teams and need standardization + guardrails.”
- “We need safe rollouts; no surprise behavior changes.”

What to run FIRST (hero scenario)
1) Reliability + Smart Routing + Fallback (Console + a scripted request)
- Show: a route policy that prefers Model A, falls back to compatible Model B when thresholds trip / capacity constrained.
- Show: canary/rollout toggles (even if we keep it simple in demo).
- Proof moment: “Your app stays online even when a model/region is degraded.”

Optional follow-on scenario (if time)
2) Observability: token-level cost & latency breakdown + error analysis
- Show: per-route/model dashboards, 5xx and throttle panels, and a trace/error view.
- Emphasize: “We make serving measurable and tunable.”

Key proof points (phrasing that lands)
- “Unified runtime + control plane: same API and operational model across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.”
- “SLO-oriented controls: routing policies, fallbacks, and safe rollouts designed for production.”
- “Cost-aware performance levers: batching/caching/quantization profiles with measurable impact.”

Questions you will get (and recommended answers)
- Q: “How do you handle model/provider outages?”
  - A: “We route by policy and have compatible fallbacks; we can also pin versions so you control change. In the demo tenant we show a fallback path and how it surfaces in dashboards.”
- Q: “Can we standardize across business units?”
  - A: “That’s a core use case: consistent API, quotas, and observability. Dedicated/Private are available when isolation/regulatory needs increase.”
- Q: “How do rollouts work?”
  - A: “Model version pinning + controlled rollout policies (canary/A-B), plus automated fallback if error/latency thresholds exceed policy.”

Console clickpath (short version)
- Console → Routes → [Demo Route] → Routing policy + fallback target
- Console → Observability → Latency / Cost dashboards (saved views)
- Console → Rollouts (if included) → show pinned version + canary toggle

Red flags / what NOT to do
- Don’t over-index on “model quality” claims for this persona; they care more about predictable behavior and operations.
- Don’t improvise on pricing; stick to “unit economics are tunable; we’ll validate with your workload.”

Success criteria to capture before ending
- Target p95 latency + throughput target
- Regions/data residency constraints
- Required availability/SLA expectations
- What “graceful degradation” means in their system (timeouts? reduced quality? cached answers?)

Recommended next step CTA
- “Let’s run a 30–60 minute eval on your top 3 prompts + traffic shape to pick the right model + serving profile.”

========================================
Persona 2: ML Engineering / Applied ML ("make it correct + fast enough")
========================================
What they’re optimizing for
- Output quality and correctness under real production prompts.
- Reproducibility: version pinning, regression checks, and stable behavior under updates.
- Practical throughput/cost: batching/caching/quantization tradeoffs without “mystery regressions.”

Primary pain points we should mirror back
- “We can’t safely change models or quantization without breaking output.”
- “Tool calling / structured output is flaky and hard to validate.”
- “We need to see quality regressions early, not after customers complain.”
- “We need lower cost per token without losing quality.”

What to run FIRST (hero scenario)
Option A (most common): Structured output + validation + deterministic prompt set
- Show: one scripted request that returns JSON/structured fields, highlight guardrails and stability.
- Proof moment: “Engineering can rely on the response shape; less glue code and fewer production failures.”

Option B (if they care about agentic workflows): Tool calling with a controlled function signature
- Show: tool/function call in streaming mode, minimal “magic,” emphasize exact schema and observability.
- Proof moment: “You can trace what happened, and failures are debuggable.”

Optional follow-on scenario (if time)
- Cost/performance tuning: batching/caching configuration suggestions + impact on token cost and latency.

Key proof points (phrasing that lands)
- “Pin model versions + serving profiles so behavior doesn’t drift under you.”
- “Operational tooling built for ML workflows: rollouts, A/B, and regression-friendly prompt sets/evals.”
- “Optimization is not a black box: we show per-token cost/latency, and you can choose the tradeoffs.”

Questions you will get (and recommended answers)
- Q: “How do you prevent quality regressions when you optimize?”
  - A: “We pin versions and can roll changes through canary/A-B. We recommend validating with your prompt sets/evals before switching profiles.”
- Q: “Do you support streaming + tool calling + structured output?”
  - A: “Yes—our demo scenarios include streaming, tool calling, and structured output, plus what happens when validation fails.”
- Q: “Can we bring our own model?”
  - A: “We support multiple deployment modes; in Dedicated/Private we can accommodate customer requirements depending on architecture and licensing. For the demo we use curated models with verified performance profiles.”

Console clickpath (short version)
- Console → API Playground (or scenario runner) → run structured output request
- Console → Observability → request trace / error analysis
- Console → Models → pinned version + serving profile details (keep it high-level)

Red flags / what NOT to do
- Don’t position Redwood as “a research lab” or “a new model provider.” Keep focus: serving + predictable operations + economics.
- Don’t claim universal best latency for all prompts. Use: “We optimize by workload shape; we’ll benchmark your distribution.”

Success criteria to capture before ending
- Their “must not break” output contracts (schemas, tool signature expectations)
- Evaluation methodology (gold set? human review? offline metrics?)
- Traffic distribution (sequence lengths, concurrency) and acceptable fallback behavior

Recommended next step CTA
- “We’ll run an eval + performance benchmark on your prompt set; we’ll propose a pinned version + rollout plan that minimizes regression risk.”

========================================
Persona 3: Security / Compliance / Procurement-adjacent ("make it safe + auditable")
========================================
What they’re optimizing for
- Data handling: retention, logging, encryption, access controls.
- Isolation: tenancy boundaries, dedicated capacity, private networking.
- Auditability: audit logs, incident response, governance.

Primary pain points we should mirror back
- “We can’t put sensitive data into a public endpoint without controls.”
- “We need clear retention + deletion. Who can see prompts/outputs?”
- “We require SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, KMS integration.”
- “We need a private deployment path if/when we expand.”

What to run FIRST (hero scenario)
Security posture walkthrough (fast, concrete)
- Start with the Demo Tenant Security FAQ highlights:
  - demo tenant is sanitized (no customer data)
  - access-controlled; credentials handled intentionally; least-privilege
  - logging posture and what is/is not retained in demo
  - encryption in transit/at rest (high-level)
- THEN show a small, safe API call (non-sensitive prompt) just to prove “it’s real.”

Optional follow-on scenario (if time)
- Private/VPC narrative + “same interface” claim
  - Show: how the same API/config maps to Private deployment mode (keep it conceptual; do not promise timelines).

Key proof points (phrasing that lands)
- “Deployment flexibility is a security feature: Hosted for speed, Dedicated for isolation, Private for regulated workloads.”
- “Access controls + auditability are first-class, not an afterthought.”
- “We can align retention and logging with your policy (and keep demo tenant sanitized).”

Questions you will get (and recommended answers)
- Q: “Do you train on our data?”
  - A: “We do not use customer inputs to train models. For the demo tenant, we only use synthetic prompts and sanitized content.”
- Q: “What’s your retention policy?”
  - A: “We have configurable retention/logging options by plan/deployment mode; for this demo tenant, logging is restricted and sanitized. We can share the detailed policy in the security package/FAQ.”
- Q: “Can you do VPC / on-prem / data residency?”
  - A: “Yes—Private deployments support customer-managed networking and region constraints. If residency is a hard requirement, we’ll scope regions early.”
- Q: “Do you support SSO/SAML and RBAC?”
  - A: “Yes; and we restrict demo tenant access to internal users. Prospect access is via controlled workflows (not ad hoc).”

Console clickpath (short version)
- Console → Settings/Security (RBAC/SSO references if available in demo)
- Console → Audit/Activity logs (if enabled in demo tenant) OR show prepared slide/screenshot
- Console → Deployment modes slide (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) with “what changes / what stays the same”

Red flags / what NOT to do
- Don’t hand-wave about compliance. If you don’t know, say: “We’ll follow up with Naomi/Marcus and provide the approved security packet.”
- Don’t show any logs that could contain sensitive content (even synthetic) without checking the demo tenant logging setting first.

Success criteria to capture before ending
- Required compliance (SOC2, etc.), audit requirements, and timelines
- Data residency constraints (EU-only, US-only)
- Whether they require Private/VPC from day 1 vs later

Recommended next step CTA
- “Security review track: we’ll share the security FAQ + schedule a 30-min security deep dive; in parallel we can run a sandbox eval with sanitized prompts.”

========================================
Mixed audience guidance (common in enterprise calls)
========================================
If you have Platform Eng + Security:
- Start Security posture (3–5 min) so the call doesn’t derail.
- Then run Reliability/Fallback + dashboards (hero) to keep technical credibility.

If you have ML Eng + Platform Eng:
- Start Structured output/tool calling (prove correctness) then pivot to operability + cost/latency controls.

If Procurement shows up unexpectedly:
- Do not discuss pricing details. Use: “We price by usage / reserved capacity; we’ll scope after we confirm deployment mode and traffic.” Point them to the right follow-up.

========================================
Scenario mapping (cheat sheet)
========================================
Scenario → Best persona fit → What it proves
- Streaming chat (fast) → Platform + ML → real-time behavior, latency, developer UX
- Structured output (JSON) → ML → correctness, contract reliability, reduced integration risk
- Tool calling (function) → ML + Platform → controllable agent behavior + debuggability
- Routing + fallback → Platform → reliability + graceful degradation
- Token cost & latency dashboards → Platform + Procurement-adjacent → transparency and tunability of serving economics
- Private/VPC narrative → Security + Platform → deployment flexibility + control

========================================
Prep checklist (2 minutes before the call)
========================================
- Confirm which persona is primary (who asked for the meeting?)
- Pick hero scenario + one backup
- Verify demo tenant is “green” (latency/errors) per dashboards
- Ensure the prompts used are the approved, sanitized set
- Have the relevant follow-up links ready:
  - Security FAQ
  - Quickstart / sample curl scripts
  - Next-step eval plan outline
